options: A single-owner value stored on the heap
quiz.explain: `Box<T>` puts one value on the heap with a single owner. It's needed for large values and for recursive types whose size would otherwise be unknown.

options: Makes a deep copy of the underlying data
Adds another owner and bumps the reference count (cheap, no data copy)
Moves the value to a new thread
quiz.explain: `Rc::clone` is cheap: it creates another handle pointing at the same data and increments the owner count. The data itself is shared, not duplicated.

quiz.q: You need several threads to share ownership of one value. Which do you use?
quiz.explain: `Arc<T>` is the thread-safe reference-counted pointer. `Rc<T>` isn't thread-safe and won't compile across threads; use `Arc` when threads are involved.

quiz.q: Why is `Box` required for a recursive type like a linked-list node?
options: Because recursion is not allowed in Rust
A Box is pointer-sized, giving the type a finite, known size the compiler can compute
Because Box makes it run faster
It isn't required; recursive types work without any indirection
quiz.explain: Without indirection, a node containing itself would have infinite size. A `Box` is a fixed-size pointer, so the compiler can finally compute the type's size.

flashcards.back: Single owner, value on the heap. Use for large values and recursive types (like linked lists) where the size must be finite and known.
Multiple owners of one value, single-threaded. `Rc::clone` bumps an owner count cheaply; the value drops when the last owner goes away.
Same idea; `Arc` uses a thread-safe (atomic) counter so it can be shared across threads. `Rc` is single-threaded and slightly faster.
Not directly — they give shared read access. Combine with `RefCell` (single-thread) or `Mutex` (multi-thread) to mutate shared data.
